claim: Parasitic helminths use two benzoquinones as electron carriers in the electron transport chain.
source: Parasitic helminths use two benzoquinones as electron carriers in the electron transport chain.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about helminth metabolism.

claim: In normoxia, parasitic helminths use ubiquinone (UQ).
source: In normoxia, they use ubiquinone (UQ), but in anaerobic conditions inside the host, they require rhodoquinone (RQ) and greatly increase RQ levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the broader literature on helminth metabolism.

claim: In anaerobic conditions inside the host, parasitic helminths require rhodoquinone (RQ) and greatly increase RQ levels.
source: In normoxia, they use ubiquinone (UQ), but in anaerobic conditions inside the host, they require rhodoquinone (RQ) and greatly increase RQ levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the broader literature on helminth metabolism.

claim: The switch from UQ to RQ synthesis is driven by a change of substrates by the polyprenyltransferase COQ-2.
source: We previously showed the switch from UQ to RQ synthesis is driven by a change of substrates by the polyprenyltransferase COQ-2 (Del Borrello et al., 2019; Roberts Buceta et al., 2019); however, the mechanism of substrate selection is not known.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Helminths synthesize two coq-2 splice forms, coq-2a and coq-2e.
source: Here, we show helminths synthesize two coq-2 splice forms, coq-2a and coq-2e, and the coq-2e-specific exon is only found in species that synthesize RQ.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by RNA-seq and genome analysis.

claim: The coq-2e-specific exon is only found in species that synthesize RQ.
source: Here, we show helminths synthesize two coq-2 splice forms, coq-2a and coq-2e, and the coq-2e-specific exon is only found in species that synthesize RQ.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by comparative genomic analysis across multiple species.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, COQ-2e is required for efficient RQ synthesis.
source: We show that in Caenorhabditis elegans COQ-2e is required for efficient RQ synthesis and survival in cyanide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from CRISPR-engineered mutants and LC-MS quantitation.

claim: COQ-2e is required for survival in cyanide in C. elegans.
source: We show that in Caenorhabditis elegans COQ-2e is required for efficient RQ synthesis and survival in cyanide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from KCN recovery assays.

claim: Parasites switch from COQ-2a to COQ-2e as they transit into anaerobic environments.
source: Importantly, parasites switch from COQ-2a to COQ-2e as they transit into anaerobic environments.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of different life stages in Ascaris suum and Strongyloides stercoralis.

claim: Helminths switch from UQ to RQ synthesis principally via changes in the alternative splicing of coq-2.
source: We conclude helminths switch from UQ to RQ synthesis principally via changes in the alternative splicing of coq-2.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Soil-transmitted helminths (STHs) such as Ascaris, hookworms, and whipworms infect well over a billion people.
source: Soil-transmitted helminths (STHs) such as Ascaris, hookworms, and whipworms infect well over a billion people, and 7 out of the 18 neglected diseases categorized by WHO are caused by helminths (CDC, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to CDC data.

claim: 7 out of the 18 neglected diseases categorized by WHO are caused by helminths.
source: Soil-transmitted helminths (STHs) such as Ascaris, hookworms, and whipworms infect well over a billion people, and 7 out of the 18 neglected diseases categorized by WHO are caused by helminths (CDC, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to CDC data.

claim: There are few classes of available anthelmintics and resistance is increasing in humans.
source: Despite the huge impact on global health of these infections, there are few classes of available anthelmintics and resistance is increasing in humans and is widespread in some species that infect animals — for example, Haemonchus contortus, a common parasite in small ruminants, has developed multidrug resistance (Jackson and Coop, 2000; Kotze and Prichard, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature on anthelmintic resistance.

claim: Haemonchus contortus has developed multidrug resistance.
source: Despite the huge impact on global health of these infections, there are few classes of available anthelmintics and resistance is increasing in humans and is widespread in some species that infect animals — for example, Haemonchus contortus, a common parasite in small ruminants, has developed multidrug resistance (Jackson and Coop, 2000; Kotze and Prichard, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature on anthelmintic resistance.

claim: When STHs are in the free-living stages of their life cycles, they use the same aerobic respiration as their hosts and use ubiquinone (UQ) as an electron carrier in their mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC).
source: When STHs are in the free-living stages of their life cycles, they use the same aerobic respiration as their hosts and use ubiquinone (referred to here as UQ and as Q in other papers) as an electron carrier in their mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of helminth metabolism.

claim: Ascaris can live for many months in the anaerobic environment of the host gut.
source: This is particularly the case for species that inhabit the host gut, for example Ascaris can live for many months in this anaerobic environment (Dold and Holland, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: RQ is an electron carrier that functions in the mitochondrial ETC of STHs.
source: RQ is an electron carrier that functions in the mitochondrial ETC of STHs (Van Hellemond et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: RQ is a prenylated aminobenzoquinone that is similar to UQ.
source: RQ is a prenylated aminobenzoquinone that is similar to UQ (Figure 1), but the slight difference in structure gives RQ a lower standard redox potential than UQ (−63 mV and 110 mV, respectively) (Erabi et al., 1976; Unden and Bongaerts, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1 showing the chemical structures.

claim: RQ has a lower standard redox potential than UQ (−63 mV and 110 mV, respectively).
source: RQ is a prenylated aminobenzoquinone that is similar to UQ (Figure 1), but the slight difference in structure gives RQ a lower standard redox potential than UQ (−63 mV and 110 mV, respectively) (Erabi et al., 1976; Unden and Bongaerts, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: In aerobic metabolism, UQ can accept electrons from a diverse set of molecules via quinone-coupled dehydrogenases, including succinate dehydrogenase and electron-transferring-flavoprotein (ETF) dehydrogenase.
source: In aerobic metabolism, UQ can accept electrons from a diverse set of molecules via quinone-coupled dehydrogenases, including succinate dehydrogenase and electron-transferring-flavoprotein (ETF) dehydrogenase.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of mitochondrial metabolism.

claim: In RQ-dependent anaerobic metabolism, RQ carries electrons to dehydrogenase enzymes and drives them in reverse to act as reductases that transfer electrons onto a diverse set of terminal acceptors.
source: In RQ-dependent anaerobic metabolism, RQ does the reverse — it carries electrons to these same dehydrogenase enzymes and drives them in reverse to act as reductases that transfer electrons onto a diverse set of terminal acceptors (Tielens and Van Hellemond, 1998; van Hellemond et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The difference in the direction of electron flow between UQ and RQ is driven by the difference in redox potential.
source: UQ thus allows electrons to enter the ETC via dehydrogenases; RQ can drive the reactions that let electrons leave the ETC and this difference in the direction of electron flow is driven by the difference in redox potential (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: RQ-dependent metabolism does not occur in the hosts and is thus an excellent target for anthelmintics.
source: This RQ-dependent metabolism does not occur in the hosts and is thus an excellent target for anthelmintics (Kita et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a logical inference about drug targeting.

claim: Among animals, RQ has only been described in nematodes, platyhelminths, mollusks, and annelids.
source: Among animals, RQ has only been described in nematodes, platyhelminths, mollusks, and annelids (Van Hellemond et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: In contrast to bacteria, where RQ derives from UQ, RQ biosynthesis in animals requires precursors derived from tryptophan.
source: In contrast to bacteria, where RQ derives from UQ (Bernert et al., 2019; Brajcich et al., 2010), RQ biosynthesis in animals requires precursors derived from tryptophan (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: C. elegans strains carrying mutations in kynu-1 are unable to synthesize RQ.
source: Recent studies performed on C. elegans have demonstrated that animals that lack a functional kynureninase pathway (e.g. strains carrying mutations in kynu-1, the sole kynureninase) are unable to synthesize RQ (Del Borrello et al., 2019; Roberts Buceta et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (3HA) from the kynurenine pathway is presumed to be prenylated in a reaction catalyzed by COQ-2.
source: It is presumed that 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (3HA, also sometimes referred to as 3HAA) from the kynurenine pathway is prenylated in a reaction catalyzed by COQ-2.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous studies and the known pathway.

claim: The critical choice between UQ and RQ synthesis is the choice of substrate by COQ-2.
source: The key insight from these previous studies is that the critical choice between UQ and RQ synthesis is the choice of substrate by COQ-2 — if 4HB is prenylated by COQ-2, UQ will ultimately be produced, but if 3HA is used, the final product will be RQ.
evidence: This is based on previous studies by the authors.

claim: If 4HB is prenylated by COQ-2, UQ will ultimately be produced.
source: The key insight from these previous studies is that the critical choice between UQ and RQ synthesis is the choice of substrate by COQ-2 — if 4HB is prenylated by COQ-2, UQ will ultimately be produced, but if 3HA is used, the final product will be RQ.
evidence: This is based on previous studies by the authors.

claim: If 3HA is prenylated by COQ-2, the final product will be RQ.
source: The key insight from these previous studies is that the critical choice between UQ and RQ synthesis is the choice of substrate by COQ-2 — if 4HB is prenylated by COQ-2, UQ will ultimately be produced, but if 3HA is used, the final product will be RQ.
evidence: This is based on previous studies by the authors.

claim: In most parasitic helminths, there is a major shift in quinone composition as they move from aerobic to anaerobic environments.
source: In most parasitic helminths, there is a major shift in quinone composition as they move from aerobic to anaerobic environments, for example, RQ is less than 10% of H. contortus total quinone when the parasite is in an aerobic environment but is over 80% of total quinone in the anaerobic environment of the sheep gut and similar shifts occur in other parasites (Lümmen et al., 2014; Sakai et al., 2012; Van Hellemond et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: RQ is less than 10% of H. contortus total quinone when the parasite is in an aerobic environment but is over 80% of total quinone in the anaerobic environment of the sheep gut.
source: In most parasitic helminths, there is a major shift in quinone composition as they move from aerobic to anaerobic environments, for example, RQ is less than 10% of H. contortus total quinone when the parasite is in an aerobic environment but is over 80% of total quinone in the anaerobic environment of the sheep gut and similar shifts occur in other parasites (Lümmen et al., 2014; Sakai et al., 2012; Van Hellemond et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: C. elegans coq-2 has two distinct splice forms: coq-2a and coq-2e.
source: We identified two distinct splice forms of C. elegans coq-2: coq-2a and coq-2e.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq and other validation studies.

claim: The two coq-2 isoforms differ by the mutually exclusive splicing of two internal exons (6a and 6e), both of 134 nucleotides.
source: These two isoforms differ by the mutually exclusive splicing of two internal exons (6a and 6e), both of 134 nucleotides (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutually exclusive splicing of cassette exons is very rare in the C. elegans genome and fewer than 100 such splicing events have been identified.
source: We note that mutually exclusive splicing of cassette exons is very rare in the C. elegans genome and fewer than 100 such splicing events have been identified (Kuroyanagi et al., 2014; Ramani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Both coq-2a and coq-2e splice forms are abundant in C. elegans across all stages of development, where ~30–50% of coq-2 is the coq-2e isoform.
source: Both coq-2a and coq-2e splice forms are abundant in C. elegans across all stages of development, where ~30–50% of coq-2 is the coq-2e isoform (Gerstein et al., 2010; Grün et al., 2014; Ramani et al., 2011; Roach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to RNA-seq and transcriptome studies.

claim: The splicing change in coq-2 causes a switch in two α-helices at the core of the COQ-2 structure.
source: We found that the splicing change causes a switch in two α-helices at the core of the COQ-2 structure (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The region switched by alternative splicing is believed to form a hydrophobic tunnel along which aromatic substrates must pass to the active site for the key polyprenylation reaction.
source: This is a region of the protein that is believed to form a hydrophobic tunnel along which aromatic substrates must pass to the active site for the key polyprenylation reaction (Desbats et al., 2016), suggesting that the change in splicing could affect COQ-2 substrate selection and thus could explain a shift from UQ to RQ synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to structural studies.

claim: All parasites known to synthesize RQ have a similar gene structure with the same mutually exclusive exons as C. elegans coq-2.
source: Remarkably, we find a similar gene structure with the same mutually exclusive exons in all parasites known to synthesize RQ (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by genome and RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Annelids and mollusks are the only other phyla known to synthesize RQ and their coq-2 orthologs also show similar mutually exclusive alternative splicing of homologous exons.
source: Furthermore, annelids and mollusks are the only other phyla known to synthesize RQ and their coq-2 orthologs also show similar mutually exclusive alternative splicing of homologous exons and we only find evidence for alternative splicing between a coq-2a form and a coq-2e like form in animals that synthesize RQ.
evidence: This is supported by genome and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: No mammalian hosts show any evidence for mutually exclusive alternative splicing of their coq-2 orthologs, nor do they have an e-like exon.
source: Crucially, no mammalian hosts show any evidence for this kind of alternative splicing of their coq-2 orthologs, nor do they have an e-like exon either in their gene predictions or genome sequences or in any available RNA-seq or direct transcriptome sequence data (human and mouse are shown as representatives in Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by genome and RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The e-exon and the mutually exclusive alternative splicing of coq-2 is unique to animals that synthesize RQ and is not found in any other species.
source: We conclude that the e-exon and the mutually exclusive alternative splicing of coq-2 is unique to animals that synthesize RQ and is not found in any other species.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: All the coq-2a-specific exons are similar to the pan-eukaryotic COQ-2 sequence, whereas all the coq-2e-specific exons have a distinct sequence to this.
source: We find that all the coq-2a-specific exons are similar to the pan-eukaryotic COQ-2 sequence, whereas all the coq-2e-specific exons have a distinct sequence to this.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Two residues (Phe204 and Ala243 in C. elegans numbering) that are strictly conserved in pan-eukaryotic COQ-2 sequences are switched to a Leu and a Ser residue in all COQ2-e-specific exons.
source: We examined the alignments of the a- and e-specific exons and identified two residues that are strictly conserved in pan-eukaryotic COQ-2 sequences, Phe204 and Ala243 (C. elegans numbering), that are switched to a Leu and a Ser residue in all COQ2-e-specific exons that we examined (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The residues Phe204 and Ala243 sit very close to the substrates in the active site of the COQ-2 enzyme.
source: These residues sit very close to the substrates in the active site of the enzyme (Figure 2C) and we note that mutation of the equivalent Ala243 residue dramatically affects the ability of human COQ-2 to synthesize UQ (Desbats et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 2C and supported by a citation.

claim: Mutation of the equivalent Ala243 residue dramatically affects the ability of human COQ-2 to synthesize UQ.
source: These residues sit very close to the substrates in the active site of the enzyme (Figure 2C) and we note that mutation of the equivalent Ala243 residue dramatically affects the ability of human COQ-2 to synthesize UQ (Desbats et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The coq-2∆6e strain synthesizes essentially no detectable RQ but has higher levels of UQ.
source: We find that the coq-2∆6e strain synthesizes essentially no detectable RQ but has higher levels of UQ, whereas coq-2∆6a has greatly reduced UQ levels but higher RQ levels (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS quantitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The coq-2∆6a strain has greatly reduced UQ levels but higher RQ levels.
source: We find that the coq-2∆6e strain synthesizes essentially no detectable RQ but has higher levels of UQ, whereas coq-2∆6a has greatly reduced UQ levels but higher RQ levels (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS quantitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The coq-2e isoform, which includes the helminth/annelid/mollusc-specific exon 6e, is required for efficient RQ synthesis.
source: We conclude that the coq-2e isoform, which includes the helminth/annelid/mollusc-specific exon 6e, is required for efficient RQ synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from CRISPR mutants.

claim: Wild-type C. elegans can survive a 15 hr exposure to KCN.
source: We previously showed that when C. elegans is exposed to KCN, it switches to RQ-dependent metabolism and that while wild-type worms can survive a 15 hr exposure to KCN, C. elegans strains that do not synthesize RQ cannot survive.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: C. elegans strains that do not synthesize RQ cannot survive 15 hr exposure to KCN.
source: We previously showed that when C. elegans is exposed to KCN, it switches to RQ-dependent metabolism and that while wild-type worms can survive a 15 hr exposure to KCN, C. elegans strains that do not synthesize RQ cannot survive.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The coq-2∆6a strain (that can synthesize RQ) survives 15 hr of KCN exposure as well as wild-type animals.
source: We found that while the coq-2∆6a strain (that can synthesize RQ) survives 15 hr of KCN exposure, as well as wild-type animals, the coq-2∆6e strain that synthesizes no RQ does not survive, confirming the functional relevance of the coq-2e isoform as being critical for RQ synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by KCN recovery assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The coq-2∆6e strain that synthesizes no RQ does not survive 15 hr of KCN exposure.
source: We found that while the coq-2∆6a strain (that can synthesize RQ) survives 15 hr of KCN exposure, as well as wild-type animals, the coq-2∆6e strain that synthesizes no RQ does not survive, confirming the functional relevance of the coq-2e isoform as being critical for RQ synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by KCN recovery assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ascaris suum has a relatively simple life cycle where eggs are laid in the host and emerge via defecation and the L1-L3 larval stages develop within the egg outside the host.
source: Ascaris suum has a relatively simple life cycle (schematic Figure 6A) and is the pig equivalent of Ascaris lumbricoides which infects ~900 M humans. Eggs are laid in the host and emerge via defecation and the L1-L3 larval stages develop within the egg outside the host.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Ascaris life cycle and illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: Ascaris suum is the pig equivalent of Ascaris lumbricoides which infects ~900 M humans.
source: Ascaris suum has a relatively simple life cycle (schematic Figure 6A) and is the pig equivalent of Ascaris lumbricoides which infects ~900 M humans.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge.

claim: The free-living larval stages of Ascaris suum have relatively low RQ (~35% of total quinones).
source: The free-living larval stages have relatively low RQ (~35% of total quinones), whereas adults have high RQ ( ~100% of total quinones) (Takamiya et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Adult Ascaris suum have high RQ (~100% of total quinones).
source: The free-living larval stages have relatively low RQ (~35% of total quinones), whereas adults have high RQ ( ~100% of total quinones) (Takamiya et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: In Ascaris suum, approximately 60% of coq-2 transcripts are coq-2e in the free-living, aerobic stages but >90% is the RQ-synthesizing coq-2e form in adults.
source: We see a clear switch approximately 60% of coq-2 transcripts are coq-2e in the free-living, aerobic stages but >90% is the RQ-synthesizing coq-2e form in adults (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In Strongyloides stercoralis, <20% of coq-2 transcripts are coq-2e in the free-living L3s but >60% is the RQ-synthesizing coq-2e form in L3s that developed inside the host.
source: The difference is clear about <20% of coq-2 transcripts are coq-2e in the free-living L3s but >60% is the RQ-synthesizing coq-2e form in L3s that developed inside the host (Figure 6D; Stoltzfus et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Increased inclusion of the coq-2e-specific exon correlates with increased synthesis of RQ during the parasite life cycles.
source: We conclude that increased inclusion of the coq-2e-specific exon correlates with increased synthesis of RQ during the parasite life cycles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RNA-seq analysis of different life stages.

claim: Animal species that synthesize RQ regulate the choice between synthesizing UQ and RQ by alternative splicing of the polyprenyltransferase COQ-2 gene.
source: In summary, our data show that animal species that synthesize RQ regulate the choice between synthesizing UQ and RQ by alternative splicing of the polyprenyltransferase COQ-2 gene.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: A switch between two mutually exclusive exons changes the core of the COQ-2 enzyme and switches it from primarily generating UQ precursors to primarily RQ precursors.
source: A switch between two mutually exclusive exons changes the core of the COQ-2 enzyme and switches it from primarily generating UQ precursors to primarily RQ precursors.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and experimental data.

claim: This alternative splicing event is only seen in species that synthesize RQ.
source: This alternative splicing event is only seen in species that synthesize RQ and the switch correlates with the change from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism in parasitic helminths.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The switch in coq-2 splicing correlates with the change from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism in parasitic helminths.
source: This alternative splicing event is only seen in species that synthesize RQ and the switch correlates with the change from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism in parasitic helminths.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of different life stages.

claim: Humans rapidly switch to anaerobic glycolysis, generating lactate, in response to hypoxia.
source: For example, humans rapidly switch to anaerobic glycolysis, generating lactate; goldfish on the other hand can adapt to hypoxia by fermenting carbohydrates to generate ethanol (Shoubridge and Hochachka, 1980).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of human metabolism.

claim: Goldfish can adapt to hypoxia by fermenting carbohydrates to generate ethanol.
source: For example, humans rapidly switch to anaerobic glycolysis, generating lactate; goldfish on the other hand can adapt to hypoxia by fermenting carbohydrates to generate ethanol (Shoubridge and Hochachka, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Only helminths, mollusks, and annelids are known to synthesize and use RQ among animal species.
source: The ability to use RQ is highly restricted among animal species — only helminths, mollusks, and annelids are known to synthesize and use RQ.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: C. elegans is a free-living nematode that does not face extended anaerobic conditions as an obligate part of its life cycle.
source: C. elegans is a free-living nematode that does not face extended anaerobic conditions as an obligate part of its life cycle.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of C. elegans biology.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a natural pathogen of C. elegans, uses cyanide to kill the worm.
source: However, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a natural pathogen of C. elegans, uses cyanide to kill the worm (Gallagher and Manoil, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Cyanide blocks the conventional ETC at Complex IV preventing the use of oxygen as a final electron acceptor.
source: Cyanide blocks the conventional ETC at Complex IV preventing the use of oxygen as a final electron acceptor.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cyanide toxicity.

claim: In C. elegans, the alternative ETC may be an adaptive strategy to withstand transient cyanide stress from pathogens.
source: We speculate that in C. elegans, the alternative ETC may be an adaptive strategy to withstand transient cyanide stress from pathogens.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors.

claim: For parasitic helminths like Ascaris, the need to respire anaerobically is critical for their life cycle since they must survive for long periods in the anaerobic environment of the human gut.
source: For parasitic helminths like Ascaris, the need to respire anaerobically is critical for their life cycle since they must survive for long periods in the anaerobic environment of the human gut.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of helminth biology.

claim: If we could interfere with RQ synthesis, this would be an excellent way to target the parasite and leave the host untouched.
source: Since the host does not synthesize RQ or use RQ-dependent metabolism if we could interfere with RQ synthesis, this would be an excellent way to target the parasite and leave the host untouched.
evidence: This is a logical inference about drug targeting.

claim: Inclusion of exon 6a results in the COQ-2a enzyme that can synthesize UQ but not RQ.
source: Inclusion of exon 6a results in the COQ-2a enzyme that can synthesize UQ but not RQ; switching exon 6a for the alternative exon 6e yields COQ-2e which principally synthesizes RQ (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Switching exon 6a for the alternative exon 6e yields COQ-2e which principally synthesizes RQ.
source: Inclusion of exon 6a results in the COQ-2a enzyme that can synthesize UQ but not RQ; switching exon 6a for the alternative exon 6e yields COQ-2e which principally synthesizes RQ (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: All eukaryotes synthesize a homolog of COQ-2a.
source: All eukaryotes synthesize a homolog of COQ-2a — only the species known to synthesize RQ (helminths, annelids, and mollusks) have genomes encoding the RQ-specific exon 6e and this exon is introduced by alternative splicing in a similar mutually exclusive splicing event in all these phyla.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Only the species known to synthesize RQ (helminths, annelids, and mollusks) have genomes encoding the RQ-specific exon 6e.
source: All eukaryotes synthesize a homolog of COQ-2a — only the species known to synthesize RQ (helminths, annelids, and mollusks) have genomes encoding the RQ-specific exon 6e and this exon is introduced by alternative splicing in a similar mutually exclusive splicing event in all these phyla.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The RQ-specific exon 6e is introduced by alternative splicing in a similar mutually exclusive splicing event in helminths, annelids, and mollusks.
source: All eukaryotes synthesize a homolog of COQ-2a — only the species known to synthesize RQ (helminths, annelids, and mollusks) have genomes encoding the RQ-specific exon 6e and this exon is introduced by alternative splicing in a similar mutually exclusive splicing event in all these phyla.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The alternative splicing of COQ-2 in all animal lineages that synthesize RQ draws focus to COQ-2 as a potential anthelmintic target.
source: The alternative splicing of COQ-2 in all animal lineages that synthesize RQ draws focus to COQ-2 as a potential anthelmintic target.
evidence: This is a logical inference about drug targeting.

claim: COQ-2e is required for RQ generation and has a distinct sequence to the pan-eukaryotic COQ-2a.
source: COQ-2e is required for RQ generation and has a distinct sequence to the pan-eukaryotic COQ-2a.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and sequence analysis.

claim: All species that synthesize RQ have a pair of conserved residues in COQ-2e.
source: The switch between COQ-2a to COQ-2e causes a change in the core of the COQ-2 active site and all species that synthesize RQ have a pair of conserved residues in COQ-2e.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors that selectively target COQ-2e and not the host COQ-2 enzyme could be potent anthelmintics.
